sec.title: Objective:
sec.p: To present the initial clinical experience with tympano-stapedotomy using the new semisynthetic TORP (NSSTORP) in patients with stapes otosclerosis associated with malleus fixation and in stapedotomy revision with unusable incus, as a less invasive alternative to malleo-stapedotomy.

sec.title: Methods:
sec.p: Between June 2024 and June 2025, 6 patients (5 females, one male; mean age, 42.1 y) underwent tympano-stapedotomy at 2 tertiary referral centers: 3 primary cases with stapes otosclerosis and malleus fixation (Avellino) and 3 revision cases with incus necrosis (Siena). All procedures were performed under local anesthesia using a surgical microscope, and a 6.5-mm-long NSSTORP was implanted in every case. Pre- and postoperative audiometric evaluation included air conduction, bone conduction, and air-bone gap (ABG) at 0.5, 1, 2, and 3 kHz. The main outcome measure was postoperative ABG ≤20 dB. Follow-up ranged from 3 to 10 months (mean, 7.2 mo).

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: No patient experienced worsening of bone conduction, dizziness, or tinnitus. The pure-tone average improved from a preoperative mean of 48.9 dB (SD = 6.9) to a postoperative mean of 32.1 dB (SD = 8.4), for a mean hearing gain of 16.8 dB (SD = 4.5). The mean ABG decreased from 25.5 dB (SD = 3.8) to 11.4 dB (SD = 3.5), representing a mean improvement of 14.1 dB (SD = 3.0). A postoperative ABG of less than 20 dB was achieved in 100% of the cases.

sec.title: Conclusion:
sec.p: Tympano-stapedotomy with the NSSTORP avoids the technically demanding steps of malleo-stapedotomy and eliminates vestibular penetration.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Currently, malleo-stapedotomy is the preferred surgical technique for addressing conductive hearing loss caused by stapes otosclerosis associated with malleus fixation or stapedotomy revision with incus necrosis1–3. In 2024, to address the limitations of malleo-stapedotomy, the first author introduced a novel technique, termed tympano-stapedotomy4. The procedure requires removal of only the posterior crus, and the fenestration is created in the posterior third of the footplate. The prosthesis used is termed “new semi-synthetic TORP” (NSSTORP), composed of a synthetic shaft with a perichondrium-covered autologous cartilage head and base4,5. The base does not enter the vestibule but rests on the rim of the fenestration. The head is not attached to the malleus and is instead positioned beneath the tympanic membrane. The NSSTORP base consists of tragal cartilage, a tissue rich in elastic fibers that provides a compliant interface6. Its central portion, in contact with the perilymph through the thin (≈0.25 mm) fenestrated footplate area, generates perilymphatic pressure waves during the piston-like motion of the shaft. This mechanism does not require stapes footplate mobility.

This study presents our initial experience with tympano-stapedotomy in 3 patients affected by stapes otosclerosis associated with malleus fixation, and in 3 revision cases of stapedotomy with incus necrosis.

sec.title: NSSTORP
sec.p: The NSSTORP is composed of a synthetic shaft and cartilage head and base4,5. The cylindrical synthetic shaft has a diameter of 0.6 mm and a length ranging from 3 to 5 mm. On both ends, the shaft is fitted with a platinum blunt cylindrical tip that is 1 mm long and 0.2 mm in diameter (Fig. 1). This shaft design is patented. At present, it is not available as a prefabricated commercial device and, in this series, was assembled intraoperatively using 2 adjustable-length stapedotomy prostheses made of polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) and platinum (7 mm total length, 0.4 mm in diameter), and a Neoflon Pro 26 GA catheter (internal diameter 0.45 mm; external diameter 0.6 mm; length 19 mm)4,5. The base is a cartilage cylinder 1 mm in height and 1 mm in diameter (Fig. 1). The head is also made of cartilage, 1 mm high and 2 mm in diameter (Fig. 1). The head’s diameter allows for clear visualization of the base’s placement on the fenestration rim. Prosthesis length is selected intraoperatively from prefabricated shaft sizes (0.5-mm increments). Tragal cartilage is ideal for constructing both the head and base, as it is flat and approximately 1.1 mm thick7. It is paramount to preserve the perichondrium on both sides of the cartilage. The perichondrium provides long-term prosthesis stability through its biological integration with both the eardrum and the margins of the small fenestra8.

sec.title: Tympano-Stapedotomy
sec.p: A transcanal approach is used. The surgical steps are as follows: elevation of the tympanomeatal flap; atticotomy; assessment of malleus and stapes mobility by palpation; measurement of the distance between the tympanic membrane and the footplate; sectioning of the stapedial tendon; removal of the posterior crus; creation of a 0.6- or 0.7-mm fenestration in the posterior third of the footplate by laser or manual perforator to avoid prosthesis interference with the incus4; harvesting of tragal cartilage; construction of the NSSTORP; placement of the NSSTORP base on the fenestration rim; positioning of the prosthesis head beneath the eardrum; and repositioning of the tympanomeatal flap (Video 2, Supplemental Digital Content 2, http://links.lww.com/MAO/C403). No additional packing or blood patch is placed around the base-footplate interface, because the autologous perichondrium of the cartilaginous base acts as a biological seal during healing.

In revision of stapedotomy with incus necrosis, the residual portion of the incus is removed. In stapedotomy, the fenestration is usually created centrally, and an incus remnant may hinder perpendicular and well-aligned placement of the prosthesis. The absence of both the stapes superstructure and the incus provides a wider and more favorable surgical field, making prosthesis placement between the fenestration rim and the tympanic membrane straightforward (Video 3, Supplemental Digital Content 3, http://links.lww.com/MAO/C404).
Contraindications to tympano-stapedotomy include an overhanging facial nerve and a narrow oval niche, which prevent adequate placement of the NSSTORP base on the footplate.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Between June 2024 and June 2025, 6 patients (5 females, 1 male; mean age, 42.1 y; range, 40–47 y) were enrolled in the study. At Avellino, 3 cases of stapes otosclerosis associated with malleus fixation were treated with primary tympano-stapedotomy. At Siena, 3 revision cases with incus necrosis underwent tympano-stapedotomy. All procedures were performed under local anesthesia with the aid of a surgical microscope. In every case, a 6.5-mm-long NSSTORP was implanted. Table 1 shows preoperative audiological data. The pure-tone audiometry included air conduction, bone conduction, and ABG averaged over 0.5, 1, 2, and 3 kHz9. The main outcome measure was the mean postoperative ABG ≤20 dB. For all patients, the last audiological control was performed in July 2025. The follow-up period ranged from 3 to 10 months (mean: 7.2 mo). Patients were fully informed concerning tympano-stapedotomy, and they gave their written informed consent after a discussion of the alternatives, which included incus-stapedotomy. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (approval no. 406/2023).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: During and at the end of the follow-up period, none of the patients experienced worsening of bone conduction, dizziness, tinnitus, or taste disturbance. Preoperative and postoperative audiometric data are shown in Table 1. The changes in air-conduction PTA and word recognition score (WRS) are presented in Figures 2 and 3. A postoperative ABG ≤10 was achieved in 50% (n=3), ≤15 in 83.3% (n=5), and ≤20 in 100% (n=6).

sec.p: In patients undergoing surgery for incus necrosis, the mean postoperative ABG was 11.9 dB, whereas after initial primary stapedotomy, the ABG was 8.3 dB.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Malleo-stapedotomy has long been considered one of the most delicate and technically demanding options for treating stapes otosclerosis with malleus fixation and stapedotomy revision with unusable incus1–3. It is often reserved for experienced surgeons1–3. By contrast, tympano-stapedotomy reduces several technically demanding steps of malleo-stapedotomy and appears to be less operator-dependent, relying on a more reproducible surgical sequence.

The main challenges of malleo-stapedotomy include:
Fixation of the prosthesis to the malleus handle, which is technically difficult1–3. To simplify this step, some authors recommend an endaural approach combined with superior canaloplasty3. Others have proposed self-fixing prostheses10. However, the shape and diameter of the malleus handle vary considerably. In some cases, the malleus handle is too thick to allow proper fixation of a super-elastic nitinol prosthesis10.
Risk of prosthesis displacement from the footplate hole during tympanic membrane-malleus complex excursions caused by physiological pressure changes (eg, nose blowing, sneezing, swallowing). This risk requires deeper insertion of the prosthesis tip—typically at least 0.5 mm into the vestibule—compared to the 0.25 mm depth recommended in conventional incus-stapedotomy1–3. In incus-stapedotomy, the malleus-incus joint buffers the displacement of the prosthesis during tympanic membrane excursions. In malleo-stapedotomy, this protective buffer is absent, increasing the risk of inner ear trauma due to excessive prosthesis penetration. Reported rates of sensorineural hearing loss after malleo-stapedotomy range from 3% to 8% (mean: 6%)2.
Contact between the synthetic prosthesis and the tympanic membrane, which increases the risk of extrusion2.

The tympano-stapedotomy technique overcomes these limitations:
Simplified prosthesis placement: it does not require an endaural approach or superior canaloplasty, the removal of the malleus head, incus, and stapes superstructures, the fixation to the malleus and the introduction into vestibule. It requires only the posterior crus removal4. This maneuver is safe because the intact incudo-stapedial joint and the intact anterior crus prevent footplate luxation.
Stable coupling: during surgery, due to the high capillarity of the perichondrium, the NSSTORP base adheres firmly to the fenestration rim, and the head adheres to the eardrum, ensuring stable positioning without the need for Gelfoam. With healing, the perichondrium of the head fuses with the eardrum, and that of the base with the fenestration rim.
Improved energy transmission: the secure coupling minimizes energy loss during sound transmission. The absence of full restoration of the ossicular lever effect (≈2–3 dB) may contribute to the limited proportion of patients achieving very small postoperative air-bone gaps (≤10 and ≤15 dB) without affecting the overall functional success of the procedure.
Reduced risk of vestibular trauma: the NSSTORP is not inserted into the vestibule, eliminating the risk of damage due to over-insertion, barotrauma, endolymphatic hydrops, or tympanic membrane atelectasis.
Lower risk of extrusion: The stable interlock of the shaft tip within the head and base prevents synthetic shaft displacement and contact with the tympanic membrane, thereby minimizing the risk of extrusion.
The auditory outcomes of tympano-stapedotomy are favorable: in this limited series, 100% of patients achieved a postoperative ABG ≤20 dB (Table 1). According to published data, with the malleo-stapedotomy a postoperative ABG ≤20 dB is achieved in 69.1% to 100% of cases (mean: 83.9%)1–3

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: The synthetic NSSTORP shaft is not yet commercially available; a dedicated prefabricated prosthesis is under development and a formal regulatory process is ongoing, with the aim of making it accessible to other surgeons in the future. This study has some limitations, mainly related to the small sample size and the relatively short follow-up period.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Tympano-stapedotomy is a less invasive alternative to malleo-stapedotomy, as it avoids both the technically demanding steps of the traditional approach and the insertion of the prosthesis into the vestibule.
